title: No. 45 — The Alleged Danger From the Powers of the Union to the State Governments. Considered For the Independent Journal. Saturday, January 26, 1788 (Madison)
paragraphs: HAVING shown that none of the powers transferred to the federal government is unnecessary or improper, the next question to consider is whether the whole bundle of them will be dangerous to the share of authority left in the individual States.

The opponents of the convention's plan, instead of first considering how much power was absolutely necessary for the federal government's purposes, have exhausted themselves on a secondary inquiry into the possible consequences of the proposed degree of power for the State governments. But if the Union, as has been shown, is essential to the security of the American people against foreign danger; if it is essential to their security against rivalries and wars between the States; if it is essential to guard them against the violent and oppressive factions that poison the blessings of liberty, and against the military establishments that gradually corrupt liberty itself; if, in short, the Union is essential to the happiness of the people of America, is it not absurd to argue against a government, without which the goals of the Union cannot be reached, that such a government may diminish the importance of the State governments? Was the American Revolution fought, was the American Confederacy formed, was the precious blood of thousands shed, and the hard-earned wealth of millions spent, not so the people of America could enjoy peace, liberty, and safety, but so that individual State governments and particular local establishments could enjoy a certain measure of power and wear certain dignities and attributes of sovereignty? We have heard the impious doctrine of the Old World, that the people were made for kings, not kings for the people. Is the same doctrine to be revived in the New World in another form, holding that the solid happiness of the people must be sacrificed to the ambitions of political institutions of a different shape? It is too early for politicians to assume we have forgotten that the public good, the real welfare of the great body of the people, is the supreme object to be pursued, and that no form of government has any value except as it is suited to achieving this object. Were the convention's plan harmful to public happiness, my voice would say: Reject the plan. Were the Union itself inconsistent with public happiness, my voice would say: Abolish the Union. In the same way, as far as the sovereignty of the States cannot be reconciled to the happiness of the people, every good citizen must say: Let the former be sacrificed to the latter. How far that sacrifice is necessary has been shown. How far what remains unsacrificed will be endangered is the question before us.

Several important considerations have been touched on in the course of these papers, undermining the assumption that the federal government's operation will gradually prove fatal to the State governments. The more I turn the subject over, the more fully convinced I am that the balance is much more likely to be disturbed by the weight of the latter than the former.

We have seen, in every example of ancient and modern confederacies, the strongest tendency on the part of the member states to strip the central government of its authorities, paired with a feeble capacity in the central government to defend itself against these encroachments. In most of these examples, the system has been so different from the one under consideration that we should be cautious about drawing any inference about ours from the fate of theirs. Still, since the States will retain a very large share of active sovereignty under the proposed Constitution, we should not entirely ignore the lesson. In the Achaean league, the federal head probably had a degree and kind of power that gave it considerable resemblance to the government framed by the convention. The Lycian Confederacy, as far as its principles and form have come down to us, must have borne an even closer analogy to it. Yet history does not tell us that either of them ever degenerated, or tended to degenerate, into a single consolidated government. On the contrary, we know that the ruin of one of them came from the inability of the federal authority to prevent the dissensions, and finally the disunion, of the subordinate authorities. These cases deserve our attention all the more because the external pressures binding their parts together were much greater and more numerous than in our case. So weaker internal bonds would have been enough to hold the members to the head and to one another.

We have seen the same tendency at work in the feudal system. Despite the lack of proper sympathy in nearly every case between local sovereigns and the people, and despite occasional sympathy between the general sovereign and the people, the local sovereigns usually prevailed in the rivalry of encroachments. If external dangers had not enforced internal harmony and order, and especially if the local sovereigns had held the affections of the people, the great kingdoms of Europe would today consist of as many independent princes as there were once feudal barons.

The State governments will have the advantage over the federal government, whether we compare them by the immediate dependence of one on the other, by the weight of personal influence each side will hold, by the powers vested in each, by the people's likely preference and support, or by the disposition and ability of each to resist and frustrate the measures of the other.

The State governments may be regarded as constituent and essential parts of the federal government, while the federal government is in no way essential to the operation or organization of the State governments. Without the State legislatures' participation, the President of the United States cannot be elected at all. They must always have a great share in his appointment, and may often determine it themselves. The Senate will be elected absolutely and exclusively by the State legislatures. Even the House of Representatives, though drawn directly from the people, will be chosen heavily under the influence of the same kind of men whose influence over the people gets them elected to the State legislatures. So each of the principal branches of the federal government will owe its existence more or less to the favor of the State governments, and must therefore feel a dependence that is far more likely to produce too obsequious an attitude toward them than too overbearing one. On the other side, the parts of the State governments will in no case owe their appointment to the direct action of the federal government, and very little, if at all, to the local influence of its members.

The number of people employed under the Constitution of the United States will be much smaller than the number employed under the individual States. So there will be less personal influence on the federal side than on the State side. The members of the legislative, executive, and judicial departments of thirteen or more States, plus the justices of the peace, militia officers, ministerial officers of justice, and all the county, city, and town officers, serving more than three million people, mingled with them and personally acquainted with every class and circle, must vastly outnumber and out-influence everyone employed in the federal administration. Compare the members of the three great departments of the thirteen States, leaving out the justices of the peace from the judiciary, with the members of the corresponding departments of the single Union government. Compare the militia officers serving three million people with the military and naval officers of any establishment within the bounds of probability or even possibility. From this view alone, the advantage of the States is clearly decisive. If the federal government has revenue collectors, the State governments will have theirs too. And since the federal collectors will be mainly on the seacoast and not very numerous, while the State collectors will be spread across the country and very numerous, the advantage on this point also lies on the same side. It is true that the Confederacy may exercise the power of collecting internal as well as external taxes throughout the States. But this power will probably not be used except for supplemental revenue. The States will likely first be given the option to supply their quotas through their own collections. Any eventual collection under the immediate authority of the Union will generally be made by officers and according to rules appointed by the States themselves. Indeed, it is highly probable that in other areas, particularly the organization of judicial power, State officers will be invested with the corresponding authority of the Union. Even if separate federal collectors of internal revenue were appointed, their total influence would not begin to compare with the multitude of State officers on the other side. Within every district assigned to a federal collector, there would be at least thirty or forty, or even more, officers of various kinds, many of them people of standing and weight, whose influence would lie on the side of the State.

The powers delegated by the proposed Constitution to the federal government are few and defined. Those that remain with the State governments are numerous and indefinite. The federal powers will be exercised mainly on external matters, such as war, peace, negotiation, and foreign commerce, with which the power of taxation will mostly be connected. The powers reserved to the States will reach all the matters that, in ordinary affairs, concern the lives, liberties, and properties of the people, and the internal order, improvement, and prosperity of the State.

The federal government's operations will be most extensive and important in times of war and danger. The State governments will be most active in times of peace and security. Since the former periods will probably be a small fraction of the latter, the State governments will enjoy yet another advantage over the federal government here. In fact, the better the federal powers are made for national defense, the less frequent will be the scenes of danger that might raise the federal government's standing above the State governments.

If the new Constitution is examined accurately and fairly, it will be found that the change it proposes consists much less in adding NEW POWERS to the Union than in strengthening its ORIGINAL POWERS. The regulation of commerce, it is true, is a new power, but few oppose it and no one fears it. The powers relating to war and peace, armies and fleets, treaties and finance, along with the other major powers, are all already vested in the existing Congress by the Articles of Confederation. The proposed change does not enlarge these powers; it only substitutes a more effective way of administering them. The change related to taxation may be regarded as the most important. Yet the present Congress already has full authority to REQUIRE indefinite supplies of money from the States for the common defense and general welfare, just as the future Congress will have to require them of individual citizens. And the citizens will be no more bound to pay than the States themselves have been. If the States had complied promptly with the Articles of Confederation, or if their compliance could have been enforced by means as peaceable as those used successfully against individuals, our past experience gives little support to the view that the State governments would have lost their constitutional powers and gradually undergone full consolidation. To claim such an outcome would be to say that the existence of the State governments is incompatible with any system whatsoever that achieves the essential purposes of the Union.
